balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
Merck KGaA reports three segments: Healthcare (prescription medicines, fertility), Life Science (lab tools, bioprocessing consumables for drugmakers) and Electronics (semiconductor materials and display/OLED materials).

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: Electronics is the renamed former Performance Materials segment -- same business, new label -- and is the most cyclical of the three, swinging with the semiconductor capex cycle (it roughly doubled FY2019-FY2022 on the chip boom, then fell back FY2023-FY2025). Life Science grew sharply into FY2022 on COVID-era bioprocessing demand and has since normalised lower. Healthcare is the steadiest grower of the three.

What to watch:

  • Electronics tracking the semiconductor cycle rather than secular growth
  • Life Science reverting further from its FY2022 pandemic peak
  • Healthcare's steadier growth cushioning the other two segments' cyclicality

kgProfitWithdrawal.title: Profit withdrawal to E. Merck KG
kgProfitWithdrawal.content:
Merck KGaA is a KGaA (partnership limited by shares): the Darmstadt-based E. Merck KG, the family holding vehicle, is the general partner and controls the company (currently holding roughly the majority of voting rights) alongside public shareholders who hold non-voting-equivalent participation in economic terms via listed shares. Each year the KGaA makes a profit withdrawal payment to E. Merck KG under the partnership agreement, on top of -- and governed separately from -- the ordinary dividend paid to free-float shareholders.

For Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany: this is a related-party cash outflow that a standard dividend/buyback view of capital allocation misses entirely. It is currently disclosed for FY2024-FY2025 only (around €747m-€755m), so the time series here is short by nature, not a data gap.

What to watch:

  • The withdrawal growing faster than net income or free cash flow
  • Total cash returned to the family (withdrawal) versus to public shareholders (dividend)
